senses.gloss: Extremely and dangerously fast.
examples: They drove at *breakneck* speed down the highway.
The company has grown at a *breakneck* pace.
The movie was shot on a *breakneck* six-week schedule.

senses.gloss: Breathing hard and fast, especially after effort.
examples: She arrived *breathless* after running up the stairs.
The climb left us *breathless*.
He felt *more breathless* than usual after a short walk, so he saw a doctor.

senses.gloss: Very excited or eager, as if holding your breath.
examples: We waited in *breathless* silence for the results.
The news was full of *breathless* praise for the new phone.

form: compound — *breath* + *taking*: it takes your breath away

senses.gloss: Extremely beautiful or impressive.
examples: The view from the top is *breathtaking*.
We drove through some *breathtaking* scenery in Utah.
It was the *most breathtaking* sunset I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Surprisingly great in degree, often of something bad.
examples: The senator showed *breathtaking* arrogance.
The project went over budget by a *breathtaking* amount.

senses.gloss: With a light, pleasant wind blowing.
examples: It was a sunny, *breezy* afternoon.
The porch is *breezier* than the living room.
Bring a jacket — it gets *breezy* by the lake.

senses.gloss: Cheerful, relaxed and casual in manner or style.
examples: She writes in a *breezy*, friendly style.
His *breezy* confidence annoyed some of the older staff.

contrast: Sounds exactly like *bridle* (уздечка).

senses.gloss: Of a bride or a wedding.
examples: The *bridal* party arrived at the church at noon.
She works in a *bridal* shop in Dallas.
Her friends threw her a *bridal* shower.

contrast: *Brief* is about time or the length of what is said, not physical length: *a short rope*, never *a brief rope*. The noun *brief* (a legal document) and *briefs* (underwear) are separate words.

senses.gloss: Lasting only a short time.
examples: We had a *brief* conversation in the hallway.
The meeting was *brief*.
This year's visit was even *briefer* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Using few words.
examples: Please keep your answers *brief*.
She gave a *brief* description of the suspect.

contrast: American style guides write it open, with no hyphen after an *-ly* adverb: *brightly colored birds*. The hyphenated spelling is common but counts as an error in edited writing. American *colored*, not British *coloured*.

senses.gloss: Having strong, vivid colors.
examples: The kids wore *brightly-colored* raincoats.
Tropical fish are often *brightly colored*.
The males are *more brightly colored* than the females.

contrast: In American English *brilliant* means very clever, excellent or very bright. The British use as a general *great!* (*That's brilliant, thanks!*) sounds British to American ears.

senses.gloss: Extremely intelligent or talented.
examples: She's a *brilliant* scientist.
That was a *brilliant* idea.
He was one of the *most brilliant* students I ever taught.

senses.gloss: Very bright or vivid.
examples: The sky was a *brilliant* blue.
We woke up to *brilliant* sunshine.

senses.gloss: Excellent; extremely successful.
examples: The team had a *brilliant* season.
Her performance in the final act was *brilliant*.

position: both — mostly after a verb or a noun with *with*: *eyes brimming with tears*
form: -ing from *brim*, the top edge of a cup

senses.gloss: Full to the top with liquid.
examples: She handed me a cup *brimming* with coffee.
His eyes were *brimming* with tears.
After a week of rain, the pond was *brimming*.

senses.gloss: Full of a feeling or quality.
examples: The team is *brimming* with confidence.
The new coach is *brimming* with ideas.

senses.gloss: Quick and energetic.
examples: We took a *brisk* walk after dinner.
She set off at a *brisk* pace.
The music got *brisker* toward the end.

senses.gloss: Of weather: cold and fresh.
examples: It was a *brisk* fall morning.
The wind off the lake was *brisk*.

senses.gloss: Of business or sales: busy and active.
examples: Business at the store has been *brisk* all week.
Ticket sales were *brisk*.

senses.gloss: Of a manner: quick and practical, a little unfriendly.
examples: The nurse was *brisk* but kind.
He gave me a *brisk* nod and walked on.

senses.gloss: Hard but easily broken.
examples: Old plastic becomes *brittle* in the sun.
Calcium keeps your bones from getting *brittle*.
Cast iron is *more brittle* than steel.

senses.gloss: Easily damaged or upset; tense and not warm.
examples: The peace agreement is still *brittle*.
She gave a *brittle* laugh.

contrast: *Broad* and *wide* overlap for size (*a broad/wide river*), but *broad* is the word for *shoulders*, *smile*, *terms*, *daylight* and *accent*, and *wide* is the word for measurements: *ten feet wide*.

senses.gloss: Wide from side to side.
examples: He has *broad* shoulders.
The river is *broader* here.
She gave me a *broad* smile.

senses.gloss: Including many different things or people.
examples: The store sells a *broad* range of products.
The plan has *broad* support in Congress.
This is the *broadest* definition of the term.

senses.gloss: General, without details.
examples: In *broad* terms, the plan is simple.
Can you give me a *broad* outline of the project?

senses.gloss: Clear and obvious; of an accent, strong and noticeable.
examples: He was robbed in *broad* daylight.
She dropped a *broad* hint that she wanted a ring.
He speaks with a *broad* Texas accent.

senses.gloss: Willing to accept opinions and ways of life different from your own.
examples: My grandparents were surprisingly *broad-minded*.
She's a *broad-minded* teacher who listens to every point of view.
Young voters tend to be *more broad-minded* on social issues.

senses.gloss: Having wide shoulders.
examples: He's *broad-shouldered* and over six feet tall.
A *broad-shouldered* man blocked the doorway.
Swimmers are usually *more broad-shouldered* than runners.

contrast: *Broil* is American: to cook under strong direct heat from above, usually in the oven. British English calls this *grill*, while American *grilled* food is cooked over heat on a grill.

senses.gloss: Cooked under very strong direct heat from above.
examples: I'll have the *broiled* salmon, please.
The chicken is better *broiled* than fried.
Top the *broiled* steak with butter and herbs.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I'm broke*; informally also *broke college kids*
contrast: Informal adjective, not the past tense of *break*: *I'm broke* (no money), but *My phone is broken* (damaged); ✗ *My phone is broke* is nonstandard. *Go broke* means to lose all your money or go bankrupt.

senses.gloss: Having no money.
examples: I can't go out this weekend — I'm *broke*.
The company went *broke* in 2009.
We were flat *broke* after paying the rent.

senses.gloss: Damaged, cracked or in pieces.
examples: Watch out for the *broken* glass.
She has a *broken* arm.
The back window was *broken*.

senses.gloss: Not working.
examples: The elevator is *broken* again.
We called a plumber about the *broken* dishwasher.

senses.gloss: Of a promise, rule or agreement: not kept.
examples: Voters are tired of *broken* promises.
The *broken* treaty led to war.

senses.gloss: Of a person, family or relationship: badly hurt or ruined.
examples: He grew up in a *broken* home.
After losing his business, he was a *broken* man.
She never got over her *broken* engagement.

senses.gloss: Of a language: spoken badly and with many mistakes.
examples: He asked for directions in *broken* English.
We got by with *broken* Spanish and hand signals.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun, usually *broken down* after a verb

senses.gloss: Of a vehicle or machine: no longer working.
examples: We pushed the *broken-down* truck to the side of the road.
The bus was *broken down* on the highway for three hours.

senses.gloss: In very bad condition because of age, use or neglect.
examples: They live in a *broken-down* farmhouse.
He played a *broken-down* old boxer in the film.

form: -al from *bronchi*, the air tubes of the lungs

senses.gloss: Of the tubes that carry air into the lungs.
examples: She has a *bronchial* infection.
Smoking damages the *bronchial* tubes.
The doctor gave him an inhaler for his *bronchial* asthma.

contrast: In *a bronze statue* or *a bronze medal* the word is the noun (the metal) used as a modifier; the adjective is the color. Russian *бронзовый* covers both.

senses.gloss: Having the reddish-brown color of bronze.
examples: His arms were *bronze* from a summer of working outside.
The leaves turn *bronze* in late fall.
She wore a *bronze* dress to the gala.

form: -ing from *brood*, to think for a long time about something sad

senses.gloss: Seeming sad, serious and deep in thought.
examples: He played a *brooding* detective with a dark past.
She's quieter and *more brooding* than her sister.
His silence felt *brooding*, not calm.

senses.gloss: Dark and threatening.
examples: *Brooding* storm clouds gathered over the hills.
The old house has a *brooding* atmosphere.

senses.gloss: Slightly brown.
examples: The tap water came out *brownish*.
The grass turned *brownish* in the heat.
She has *brownish* hair with red highlights.

senses.gloss: Very hard and tiring, leaving the people involved hurt or weakened.
examples: It was a *bruising* election campaign.
The team lost after a *bruising* overtime game.
The second round of talks was even *more bruising* than the first.

contrast: Often a noun (*a brunette*), and used mostly of women; the rare masculine spelling is *brunet*. English *brunette* covers dark brown to black hair, so it matches both Russian *шатенка* and *брюнетка*.

senses.gloss: Of hair: dark brown; of a person: having dark brown hair.
examples: She dyed her hair *brunette* for the role.
Both sisters are *brunette*.
The ad showed a tall *brunette* woman in a red coat.

senses.gloss: Using few words in a way that seems rude.
examples: The receptionist was *brusque* with us.
He gave a *brusque* reply and hung up.
Her emails got *more brusque* as the deadline got closer.

contrast: False friend: Russian *брутальный* is praise for a rugged, very masculine man. English *brutal* is always negative. For the Russian sense say *rugged* or *macho*.

senses.gloss: Very cruel and violent.
examples: It was a *brutal* attack.
The dictator ran a *brutal* regime.
The war was *more brutal* than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: Very harsh, unpleasant or difficult.
examples: We had a *brutal* winter this year.
That workout was *brutal*.

senses.gloss: Direct and honest in a way that ignores people's feelings.
examples: Let me be *brutal*: your essay isn't ready.
She was known for her *brutal* honesty.

contrast: Usually a noun: *He's a brute* (грубый, жестокий человек). The adjective lives mainly in *brute force* and *brute strength*.

senses.gloss: Using only physical strength or power, without thought or skill.
examples: The thieves opened the safe by *brute* force.
He lifted the car off her with *brute* strength.
The hackers guessed the password with a *brute*-force attack.

senses.gloss: Rough, cruel and without thought or feeling, like an animal.
examples: He was a *brutish* man with a violent temper.
Life in the prison camp was short and *brutish*.
The fighting grew *more brutish* as the war went on.

senses.gloss: Of the countryside, in a pleasant, peaceful way.
examples: They moved to a *bucolic* town in Vermont.
The farm looks *bucolic*, but the work is hard.
The setting for the wedding couldn't have been *more bucolic*.

senses.gloss: Beginning to develop, often with promise.
examples: She's a *budding* artist.
Their *budding* romance was the talk of the office.
The town has a *budding* tech industry.

senses.gloss: Relating to a budget.
examples: The school district faces serious *budgetary* problems.
The project was canceled for *budgetary* reasons.
Congress must approve all *budgetary* changes.

contrast: Informal American in the sense 'muscular'. The noun *buff* means a fan: *a movie buff*, *a history buff*.

senses.gloss: Informal: having strong, well-developed muscles.
examples: He got really *buff* over the summer.
The actor has to stay *buff* for the role.
He's *more buff* now than he was in college.

senses.gloss: Pale yellowish brown.
examples: The documents came in a *buff* envelope.
The old barn was painted *buff* with white trim.

contrast: The noun *buggy* is a light carriage, a golf cart, or in American English a baby carriage.

senses.gloss: Of software: full of errors.
examples: The first version of the app was really *buggy*.
The update made the game even *buggier*.

senses.gloss: Full of insects.
examples: The campsite was hot and *buggy*.
Summer evenings by the lake get *buggy*.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun, usually *built in* after a verb

senses.gloss: Made as a fixed part of something, not separate.
examples: The kitchen has *built-in* cabinets.
Most laptops have a *built-in* camera.
Is the microphone *built in*, or do I need to buy one?

senses.gloss: Being a natural or permanent part of something.
examples: The current rules give incumbents a *built-in* advantage.
Kids seem to have a *built-in* sense of fairness.

senses.gloss: Round and fat, often in an unattractive way.
examples: The clown had a big *bulbous* nose.
The lamp has a *bulbous* glass base.
The new model looks *more bulbous* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Of or from Bulgaria, its people or its language.
examples: She grew up in a *Bulgarian* village near the Black Sea.
Is this wine *Bulgarian*?
*Bulgarian* grammar has no noun cases, unlike Russian.

senses.gloss: Sticking out in a round shape, often because of being very full.
examples: He carried a *bulging* backpack.
The cartoon cat had huge *bulging* eyes.
Her suitcase was *bulging* with souvenirs.

senses.gloss: Having bulimia, an eating disorder in which a person eats a lot and then forces themselves to vomit.
examples: She was *bulimic* all through high school.
The clinic treats *bulimic* and anorexic patients.
He had no idea his roommate was *bulimic*.

senses.gloss: Large and hard to carry or store.
examples: The old TVs were heavy and *bulky*.
You can ship *bulky* furniture for an extra fee.
The winter coat is *bulkier* than it looks online.

senses.gloss: Of a person: big and heavy.
examples: A *bulky* linebacker knocked him to the ground.
He's gotten *bulky* from lifting weights.

senses.gloss: Made so that bullets cannot go through it.
examples: The president's car has *bulletproof* glass.
Officers wear *bulletproof* vests.
The bank teller's window is *bulletproof*.

senses.gloss: Informal: impossible to fail, defeat or criticize.
examples: There's no such thing as a *bulletproof* business plan.
The team looked *bulletproof* until the playoffs.

senses.gloss: Stubborn in a stupid or unreasonable way.
examples: He's too *bullheaded* to admit he was wrong.
Her *bullheaded* refusal to compromise ended the talks.
My dad got even *more bullheaded* as he got older.

form: -ish from *bull*, an investor who expects prices to rise

senses.gloss: Of investors or markets: expecting prices to rise.
examples: Investors are *bullish* on tech stocks.
Analysts turned *more bullish* after the earnings report.

senses.gloss: Confident and optimistic about the future.
examples: The coach is *bullish* about the team's chances.
She sounded *bullish* about the future of the company.

senses.gloss: Clumsy and confused, making silly mistakes.
examples: He played a *bumbling* police officer in the movie.
The new manager seemed *bumbling* but well-meaning.
The villain in the sequel is even *more bumbling* than the first one.

senses.gloss: Of traffic: moving very slowly, with cars very close together.
examples: We sat in *bumper-to-bumper* traffic for two hours.
The freeway was *bumper-to-bumper* all the way to LA.
It's always *bumper-to-bumper* on the bridge at five.

senses.gloss: Having an uneven surface.
examples: The road to the cabin is *bumpy*.
The rash made his skin red and *bumpy*.

senses.gloss: Of a trip: shaking up and down.
examples: It was a *bumpy* flight.
The ride got *bumpier* as we climbed.

senses.gloss: Full of problems or difficulties.
examples: The company had a *bumpy* first year.
The switch to the new system has been *bumpy*.

senses.gloss: Able to float.
examples: Salt water makes you *more buoyant*.
Cork is light and *buoyant*.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and confident.
examples: She was in a *buoyant* mood after the interview.
The crowd was *buoyant* after the win.

senses.gloss: Of prices, sales or the economy: rising or staying strong.
examples: Sales stayed *buoyant* through the holidays.
The housing market is still *buoyant*.

senses.gloss: Carrying a heavy load of work, worry, debt or responsibility.
examples: Many graduates are *burdened* with student loans.
She felt *burdened* by her family's expectations.
The program helps heavily *burdened* homeowners.

senses.gloss: Causing a lot of work, worry or expense.
examples: Small businesses complain about *burdensome* regulations.
The paperwork is *burdensome*.
The new rules are even *more burdensome* than the old ones.

senses.gloss: Using too many complicated official rules and procedures.
examples: Getting a building permit is a slow, *bureaucratic* process.
The company became *more bureaucratic* as it grew.
The agency is hopelessly *bureaucratic*.

senses.gloss: Of a man: big, strong and heavy.
examples: A *burly* security guard stood at the door.
Her brothers are all tall and *burly*.
He was the *burliest* player on the team.

contrast: The country is officially *Myanmar*, and news writing often uses *Myanmar* as a modifier (*the Myanmar military*). *Burmese* is still the usual word for the language, the food and the cat breed.

senses.gloss: Of or from Burma (Myanmar), its people or its language.
examples: We had dinner at a *Burmese* restaurant in San Francisco.
The *Burmese* alphabet has round letters.
Her grandmother is *Burmese*.

contrast: Americans use *burned* for the past tense and usually for the adjective too; *burnt* is also common as an adjective, especially for food and colors (*burnt toast*, *burnt orange*).

senses.gloss: Damaged, hurt or blackened by fire or heat.
examples: The *burned* building was torn down.
His hand was badly *burned*.
Throw out the *burned* cookies.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun, usually *burned out* after a verb

senses.gloss: Exhausted and without energy or interest because of too much work or stress.
examples: Many nurses feel *burned out*.
*Burned-out* teachers are leaving the profession.
I was *more burned out* after that job than I realized.

senses.gloss: Destroyed by fire, with only the outside left.
examples: We drove past *burned-out* cars.
The *burned-out* factory has been empty for years.

senses.gloss: Of a light bulb: no longer working.
examples: Replace the *burned-out* bulb in the hallway.
Two of the streetlights on our block are *burned out*.

position: both — attributive only in the sense 'strong, urgent'

senses.gloss: On fire.
examples: Firefighters rushed into the *burning* building.
We could smell *burning* rubber.

senses.gloss: Very hot, or causing a hot, painful feeling.
examples: The sand was *burning* under our feet.
I felt a *burning* pain in my chest.

senses.gloss: Very strong or urgent.
examples: She has a *burning* desire to succeed.
The *burning* question is who will pay for it.

contrast: As a verb form Americans say *burned* (*I burned the toast*); *burnt* is mostly the adjective: *burnt toast*, *burnt orange*.

senses.gloss: Damaged or blackened by fire or heat.
examples: The kitchen smelled of *burnt* toast.
The rice is *burnt* on the bottom.
Scrape off the *burnt* bits before serving.

senses.gloss: Of a color: deep and brownish.
examples: She wore a *burnt* orange sweater.
The walls are painted a *burnt* red.

senses.gloss: Of or from Burundi, its people or its culture.
examples: Our church sponsors a *Burundian* refugee family.
*Burundian* coffee is known for its fruity flavor.
The *Burundian* runner finished second.

form: compound — *bush* + *league*, a small-town minor baseball league
contrast: Informal American, from baseball.

senses.gloss: Amateurish and unprofessional; of poor quality.
examples: That was a *bush-league* move by the referee.
The whole event felt a little *bush-league*.
Their website looks even *more bush-league* than their ads.

senses.gloss: Of hair, fur or plants: growing thickly.
examples: He has thick, *bushy* eyebrows.
The fox has a long *bushy* tail.
His beard is *bushier* than it was last year.

contrast: Russian *деловой* is usually the noun *business* as a modifier: *a business meeting*, *a business suit*. *Businesslike* describes a manner: efficient, serious and not emotional.

senses.gloss: Serious, practical and efficient.
examples: She has a calm, *businesslike* manner.
The meeting was short and *businesslike*.
His tone got *more businesslike* once we started talking about money.

contrast: Informal. In careful writing say *broken* or *caught*.

senses.gloss: Informal: broken or damaged; of a body part, injured.
examples: I've got a *busted* phone screen.
The AC is *busted* again.
He came home with a *busted* lip.

senses.gloss: Informal: caught doing something wrong.
examples: Mom found the candy wrappers, and I knew I was *busted*.
You're so *busted*!

senses.gloss: Full of people and busy activity.
examples: We walked through a *bustling* market.
The downtown area is *bustling* with tourists in summer.
The port was once the *most bustling* city on the coast.

contrast: Informal and often heard as sexist; avoid it in polite conversation.

senses.gloss: Of a woman: having large breasts.
examples: The magazine was criticized for its *busty* cartoon characters.
She was tired of being cast in *busty* blonde roles.
The dress comes in a cut for *busty* women.

contrast: Informal. Calling a woman *butch* can be offensive, though some lesbian women use it proudly about themselves.

senses.gloss: Of a woman: looking or behaving in a traditionally masculine way.
examples: She describes her style as *butch*.
She dressed *more butch* in college.

senses.gloss: Of a man: very masculine and tough-looking.
examples: He tried to look *butch* in a leather jacket.
The truck ads always feature some *butch* cowboy.

senses.gloss: Containing a lot of butter, or tasting or smelling like butter.
examples: These croissants are soft and *buttery*.
The popcorn is too *buttery* for me.
This chardonnay is *more buttery* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Very soft and smooth.
examples: The seats are covered in *buttery* leather.
She has a smooth, *buttery* voice.

comparison: not gradable — but *very button-down* in the sense 'conservative'
contrast: *A button-down* (noun) is the shirt itself. In the sense 'conservative', *button-down* and *buttoned-down* mean the same.

senses.gloss: Of a shirt collar: fastened to the shirt with small buttons.
examples: He wore a blue *button-down* shirt and khakis.
The school requires a white *button-down* shirt.
*Button-down* collars look fine without a tie.

senses.gloss: Conservative and conventional.
examples: It's a very *button-down* law firm.
He left his *button-down* office job to become a chef.

senses.gloss: Fastened with buttons.
examples: Keep your coat *buttoned* — it's freezing.
He wore a *buttoned* cardigan over his shirt.
Her shirt was *buttoned* all the way up.

senses.gloss: Conservative, formal and conventional in style or behavior.
examples: He's a *buttoned-down* accountant from Ohio.
Silicon Valley is less *buttoned-down* than Wall Street.
The bank's culture is *more buttoned-down* than a startup's.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun, often *buttoned up* after a verb

senses.gloss: Reserved and formal; not showing feelings.
examples: My father was a *buttoned-up* man who rarely laughed.
She's *more buttoned-up* at work than at home.

senses.gloss: Carefully organized and under control.
examples: The campaign runs a very *buttoned-up* operation.
By Friday every detail of the deal was *buttoned up*.

contrast: Somewhat old-fashioned and literary; like *busty*, it can sound sexist.

senses.gloss: Of a woman: with large breasts and a full, healthy-looking figure.
examples: The painting shows a *buxom* barmaid pouring beer.
Old sailors' tales describe *buxom* mermaids.
The novel's heroine is a *buxom* farm girl.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is usually the verb *buzz*: *The room was buzzing*

senses.gloss: Making a low, continuous humming sound.
examples: There's a *buzzing* noise coming from the fridge.
I kept hearing a *buzzing* sound in my ears.

senses.gloss: Full of activity and excitement.
examples: Austin has a *buzzing* music scene.
The café has a *buzzing* atmosphere on weekends.

contrast: In *let bygones be bygones* (кто старое помянет) the word is a noun.

senses.gloss: From a time long past.
examples: The hotel reminds me of a *bygone* era.
These photos show the farms of *bygone* days.
The shop sells toys from a *bygone* age.

comparison: not gradable — but *more byzantine* in the sense 'complicated'
contrast: In the sense 'too complicated' it is often written with a small *b*: *byzantine tax rules*.

senses.gloss: Of the Byzantine Empire, its art or its church.
examples: The museum has a room full of *Byzantine* mosaics.
Constantinople was the capital of the *Byzantine* Empire.

senses.gloss: Very complicated and hard to understand, often secretive.
examples: The tax code is *byzantine*.
Getting a visa involves *Byzantine* rules and endless paperwork.

takes: *about* + noun (what someone will not talk about)
contrast: Also spelled *cagy*.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to give information.
examples: He was *cagey* about his plans.
The company has been *cagey* about the sales numbers.
She got even *cagier* when I asked about her ex.

senses.gloss: Clever and careful, especially from experience.
examples: The *cagey* veteran pitcher fooled the young hitters.
She's a *cagey* negotiator.

senses.gloss: Causing great damage or suffering; disastrous.
examples: The flood had *calamitous* effects on local farms.
Cutting the budget now would be *calamitous*.
The second decision proved even *more calamitous* than the first.

contrast: *Calculated* describes a plan or act; *calculating* describes a person who plans selfishly: *a calculated move* by *a calculating politician*.

senses.gloss: Carefully and deliberately planned to have a particular effect.
examples: The remark was a *calculated* insult.
The ad is *calculated* to appeal to teenagers.
Her decision to leave was cold and *calculated*.

senses.gloss: Of a risk: taken after thinking carefully about what could happen.
examples: Starting the business was a *calculated* risk.
The coach took a *calculated* gamble in the fourth quarter.

contrast: *Calculating* is a person who plans selfishly; *calculated* is the plan or act.

senses.gloss: Planning carefully to get what you want, often without caring about others.
examples: She's a cold, *calculating* businesswoman.
Behind his friendly smile, he was *calculating* and ruthless.
Her brother was even *more calculating* than she was.

senses.gloss: Of an instrument: adjusted to measure accurately.
examples: Make sure the scale is properly *calibrated*.
The lab uses only *calibrated* thermometers.

senses.gloss: Carefully planned or measured for a particular effect.
examples: The White House gave a carefully *calibrated* response.
Her speech was finely *calibrated* to please both sides.

contrast: For products and places Americans more often use the noun as a modifier: *California wine*, *the California coast*. *Californian* is common for people and style.

senses.gloss: Of or from California.
examples: She has a relaxed *Californian* attitude.
The restaurant serves *Californian* cuisine.
Her husband is *Californian*, but she's from Maine.

contrast: *Callous* (unkind) sounds the same as the noun *callus* (мозоль). Hands with hard skin are *calloused*, not *callous*.

senses.gloss: Not caring about other people's pain or problems.
examples: It was a *callous* thing to say to a grieving mother.
Officials seemed *callous* toward the victims.
The company's response was *more callous* than we feared.

contrast: Not *callous*, which means heartless.

senses.gloss: Having thick, hard skin from work or use.
examples: His hands were *calloused* from years of farm work.
Guitar players have *calloused* fingertips.
My feet were even *more calloused* after the hike.

senses.gloss: Not upset, worried or excited; peaceful.
examples: Try to stay *calm*.
She spoke in a *calm* voice.
I felt *calmer* after talking to him.

senses.gloss: Of weather or water: still, without strong wind or waves.
examples: The sea was *calm* this morning.
It was the *calmest* night of the whole trip.

comparison: not gradable — but *more caloric* in the sense 'high in calories'
contrast: For food, everyday English says *high-calorie* or *fattening* more often than *caloric*: *high-calorie snacks*.

senses.gloss: Relating to calories.
examples: Most adults need a daily *caloric* intake of about 2,000 calories.
The label lists the *caloric* content per serving.

senses.gloss: Informal: high in calories.
examples: Nuts are healthy but very *caloric*.
Fried food is *more caloric* than steamed food.

senses.gloss: Containing no calories.
examples: Water is *calorie-free*.
The soda uses a *calorie-free* sweetener.
Unfortunately, nothing that tastes this good is *calorie-free*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Cambodia, its people or its culture.
examples: Angkor Wat is the most famous *Cambodian* temple.
Long Beach has a large *Cambodian* community.
Her parents are *Cambodian*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Cameroon, its people or its culture.
examples: He plays for the *Cameroonian* national soccer team.
*Cameroonian* cooking often uses plantains and peanuts.
My roommate is *Cameroonian* and speaks French and English.

contrast: In *camouflage pants* the word is the noun used as a modifier (камуфляжный); *camouflaged* means hidden by color or shape.

senses.gloss: Hidden by colors, patterns or coverings that match the surroundings.
examples: The lizard is well *camouflaged* against the rocks.
The hunters waited in a *camouflaged* blind.
The entrance to the bunker was *camouflaged* with branches.

form: -y from *camp*, a style that enjoys exaggeration and bad taste

senses.gloss: Exaggerated and theatrical in a way that is funny or enjoyed on purpose as bad taste.
examples: We watched a *campy* 1960s horror movie.
The musical is loud, silly and *campy*.
The sequel is even *campier* than the original.

senses.gloss: Confident, positive and eager to solve problems.
examples: We love her *can-do* attitude.
The crew has a real *can-do* spirit.
He brought a *can-do* approach to the job.

contrast: American spelling has one *l*: *canceled*, *canceling*. British English doubles it: *cancelled*. *Cancellation* has two in both.

senses.gloss: Called off; no longer going to happen.
examples: We were stuck at the airport because of a *canceled* flight.
Tonight's game is *canceled* because of rain.
She got a refund for the *canceled* order.

senses.gloss: Having or being cancer.
examples: The surgeon removed a *cancerous* tumor.
Tests showed the cells were not *cancerous*.
Doctors found *cancerous* growths on his lungs.

senses.gloss: Harmful and spreading, like a disease.
examples: Corruption had a *cancerous* effect on the government.
Gossip can be *cancerous* in a small office.

senses.gloss: Honest and direct, even about difficult things.
examples: She was very *candid* about her struggle with depression.
Let me be *candid* with you.
He was *more candid* in private than in interviews.

senses.gloss: Of a photo: taken without the person posing or knowing.
examples: The wedding album is full of *candid* shots.
I like *candid* photos better than posed ones.

form: past participle of *candy*, to cook in sugar

senses.gloss: Cooked in sugar syrup and coated with sugar.
examples: The fruitcake is full of *candied* cherries.
We make *candied* yams every Thanksgiving.
Top the salad with *candied* pecans.

contrast: Also a noun: *a canine* is a dog in police or veterinary language, or a pointed tooth (клык).

senses.gloss: Relating to dogs.
examples: The police *canine* unit found the drugs.
Parvo is a serious *canine* disease.
She runs a *canine* training center.

senses.gloss: Of the pointed teeth between the front teeth and the back teeth.
examples: Humans have four *canine* teeth.
The dentist said my upper *canine* tooth is growing in crooked.

form: past participle of *can*, to put in a can
contrast: American *canned* is British *tinned*.

senses.gloss: Of food: kept in a sealed metal can.
examples: *Canned* soup is often high in salt.
We donated *canned* goods to the food bank.
Are the tomatoes fresh or *canned*?

senses.gloss: Recorded or prepared in advance, so not live or natural.
examples: The sitcom used *canned* laughter.
The spokesman gave a *canned* answer.

senses.gloss: Eating the flesh of animals of the same kind.
examples: Some spiders are *cannibalistic*.
Scientists study *cannibalistic* behavior in fish.
The horror movie is about a *cannibalistic* family in Texas.

senses.gloss: Smart and good at judging situations, especially in business or politics.
examples: She's a *canny* investor.
It was a *canny* move to sell before prices dropped.
He was the *canniest* politician in the state.

senses.gloss: Accepted as the standard, classic or official version.
examples: *Moby-Dick* is a *canonical* American novel.
This is the *canonical* example of the problem.
Fans argue about which movies are *canonical* in the series.

senses.gloss: Relating to church law or to the books accepted as part of the Bible.
examples: The four *canonical* Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
Some early Christian texts were never considered *canonical*.

senses.gloss: Bad-tempered and always complaining or arguing.
examples: My *cantankerous* old neighbor yells at kids on his lawn.
He grew *cantankerous* in his old age.
The cat got *more cantankerous* every year.

senses.gloss: Having a lot of space inside.
examples: She pulled a notebook out of her *capacious* handbag.
The SUV has a *capacious* trunk.
The *more capacious* model costs $2,000 extra.

senses.gloss: Wide in range; able to hold a lot of information or ideas.
examples: He has a *capacious* memory for baseball statistics.
The term is *capacious* enough to include almost anything.
